title: Big Brother 1: The Room Decided
subtitle: A season where power mattered, but the vote count mattered more.

winner.name: Misha
winner.keyStats: Misha won 5-4 with 2 HOH wins, 4 veto wins, 3 wins under threat, 3 times nominated, 3 times pulled off the block, 85% voting accuracy, only 1 blindside, and 5 jury votes.
winner.strategy: Misha’s winning game was not clean control; it was recoverable positioning. She kept enough relationships alive across collapsing groups that people kept needing her after they stopped trusting her. The crucial difference between Misha and the other finalists is that her comp wins came attached to danger: she repeatedly won or benefited from vetoes when her own game was exposed, then converted survival into the next vote. She was willing to be implicated in the mess, own it late, and still make the final decision that removed Joel, the finalist she believed could beat her.
winner.legacy: Misha becomes the season’s first winner as a hybrid social-competition player: not the most beloved, not the least bloodied, but the person whose game survived the most scrutiny. Her legacy is the 5-4 verdict itself — a jury split between personal loyalty to Jules and respect for Misha’s ability to keep re-entering the power structure after every rupture.

placements.name: Misha
placements.notes: Misha won because her relationships bent without fully breaking, and her veto record gave the jury a tangible reason to reward survival as agency.
placements.story: Misha’s game began as a middle-position social game inside bigger structures, but the record shows she was never just being carried by them. She voted with the house 85% of the time, was only blindsided once, and repeatedly stayed close enough to the decision-makers to know where the vote was landing. Her danger weeks were real: she was on the block three times, twice as the target, and was pulled down three times while also winning four vetoes overall. The key turn was the back half, where she stopped being merely useful and became necessary — especially once the house began aiming at bigger comp threats and visible pairs. Her final stretch was excellent: she won late HOH and veto power, survived the Joel/Jules/Tobias endgame crossfire, won the final HOH, and cut Joel because she correctly identified him as the person with the clearest jury case. The finale was messy, and several answers missed the question, but her closing argument matched the season: she made connection useful without pretending it was clean.
keyMoments: Week 5: Helped create the decisive flip that sent Zella out and owned the move when pressed.
Week 10: Won veto while nominated and removed herself from Jules's block.
Week 13: Won HOH and nominated Jane, Gyselle and Joel, forcing the endgame blocs into the open.
Week 14: Won HOH and veto, kept nominations the same, and sent Jane to jury.
Week 15: Won veto from the block, forced Tobias onto the block, and cast the sole vote to evict him.
Finale: Won Part 1 and Part 3 of the final HOH, then evicted Joel to sit beside Jules.
placements.resume: Misha could honestly argue that she survived three nominations without ever receiving an eviction vote, won six total HOH/veto competitions, won three times under threat, stayed aligned with the house on 11 of 13 votes, and made the final winning cut by removing Joel. Her case was not spotless control; it was repeated survival plus the ability to be included in the next plan after betraying the last one.
placements.demise: Misha’s last real threat was Joel at final three. He had the competition résumé, the late-game respect, and enough jurors discussing him as a serious player that sitting beside him was dangerous. Misha killed that threat by beating him in the final jury quiz tiebreaker and choosing Jules instead.
placements.optimalLine: Her correct line was the one she took: keep Jules close as the beatable-but-respected final option, use comps only when the room could no longer protect her, and cut Joel at final three even if it risked looking disloyal.

placements.name: Jules
placements.notes: Jules played the best losing finalist game: deeply connected, rarely out of the loop, but ultimately unable to turn social credit into the last jury vote.
placements.story: Jules’s finish is not an accident; the record supports a strong game. He was nominated four times, all as the target, and survived the vote every time, which means his game repeatedly passed live tests instead of theoretical ones. His social positioning was enormous — five groups, nine-person reach — and he often became the person people used to translate one room’s plan into another room’s vote. His HOH weeks mattered, especially the early Harriett/Natasha/Ireland week and the later Ireland eviction sequence, but he also let other players frame too many of those moves as shared house decisions. The jury liked him, and several jurors voted for him on personal trust, but the same loyalty that made him beloved also made his agency look softer next to Misha’s visible danger wins. He lost by one vote because the jury could see the social game, but not all of them believed it carried enough blood.
keyMoments: Week 2: Survived the block as the target after Stella left 10-3.
Week 4: Won HOH and veto, left nominations intact, and watched Harriett leave unanimously.
Week 8: Helped move the vote onto Nico after Ireland used veto, deepening his cross-room leverage.
Week 10: Won HOH, nominated Jane, Misha and Ireland, and saw Ireland leave 7-0 after Misha's veto win.
Week 12: Survived against Felipe when Gyselle, Misha and Jane moved the vote.
Finale: Chosen by Misha over Joel, then lost 5-4.
placements.resume: Jules could argue that he survived four target nominations, won two HOHs and a veto, voted correctly 78% of the time, maintained five groups across the house, and reached finale night because multiple jurors still felt personally connected to him after he betrayed them.
placements.demise: Jules lost at the jury stage because Misha’s final cut of Joel gave her a sharper strategic endpoint, while Jules’s answers leaned into relationship management without always naming the move. Felipe, Jane, Tobias and Joel rewarded him, but Dylon, Ireland, Natasha, Gyselle and Aaron decided Misha had done more to actively earn the chair.
placements.optimalLine: His best available line was to claim more ownership earlier, especially around Ireland and the mid-jury votes. The social game was real, but he needed to articulate it as control before finale night rather than asking jurors to infer it.

placements.name: Joel
placements.notes: Joel had the strongest competition résumé of the finalists but was cut because everyone understood he was the most dangerous final opponent.
placements.story: Joel’s season looks quieter socially than it was because his game often happened through pairs rather than rooms. He won 3 HOHs and 3 vetoes, including two wins under threat, and was pulled down three times when targeted. That is a real survival record, not a passenger résumé. Strategically, his issue was that his best relationships — Jules, Felipe, Tobias at different points — kept becoming visible right as the house needed an obvious reason to move. His HOH reigns produced important evictions, but several jurors questioned whether the final outcome of those weeks served Joel or the people around him. At final three, he was one question away from choosing his own opponent and likely had a very serious chance against either finalist. Misha evicting him was the clearest compliment his game received: nobody wanted to sit beside the person who could claim both comp control and late-game planning.
keyMoments: Week 2: Won veto and removed himself from Ireland's block.
Week 7: Won The Wall HOH after Jules stepped down, then nominated Dylon, Jane and Ireland.
Week 11: Won HOH and veto, kept nominations intact, and broke the tie to evict Natasha.
Week 13: Won veto while nominated and saved himself, forcing Aaron onto the block.
Week 15: Won final-four HOH and nominated Misha and Jules together.
Finale: Lost the final HOH tiebreaker to Misha and was evicted at final three.
placements.resume: Joel could have argued 6 total HOH/veto wins, three times escaping the block via veto, no eviction votes against him, several weeks where the house had to plan around his safety, and a final-three position where both remaining players saw him as too dangerous to take.
placements.demise: Misha ended Joel’s game at the final decision. After beating him in the final HOH tiebreaker, she correctly judged that his résumé and jury respect made him a losing final-two opponent for her, so she chose Jules instead.
placements.optimalLine: Joel’s best line was winning Part Three. Short of that, he needed to make Misha believe Jules had the jury locked and that Joel’s betrayals would poison his own vote count, but Misha had enough evidence to know better.

placements.name: Tobias
placements.notes: Tobias was a late-game hub and fan favorite whose loyalty-based structure collapsed one round before the finale.
placements.story: Tobias’s game was better than the pawn-chair image suggests. He was nominated five times, but three of those were pawn appearances, and his 82% voting accuracy shows he was usually in the room where the vote was decided. His six groups and ten-person reach made him one of the season’s most connected players, but the same reach made him visible as the endgame tightened. He played a strong middle-to-late game by pivoting from Dylon to Aaron to Joel/Jules when the old structures cracked, and his Block Buster win at Week 9 was a crucial self-save. The problem was that his endgame required everyone to believe he was loyal while also watching him cut Dylon, survive Jane, and build multiple final twos. Misha’s final-four veto forced him onto the block against Jules, and she chose to evict him as the last social-competition obstacle before finale.
keyMoments: Week 1: Won the first HOH, gaining early social capital despite no eviction.
Week 2: Voted out Stella despite a prior promise, establishing that sentiment would not override position.
Week 9: Won Block Buster to escape Ireland's block, allowing the house to evict Dylon.
Week 11: Survived the tied Natasha vote when Joel broke the tie in his favor.
Week 14: Survived against Jane 2-0 after Misha left nominations intact.
Week 15: Renominated after Misha used veto and evicted 1-0 by Misha.
placements.resume: Tobias could argue that he was connected to almost every major bloc, survived five nominations, saved himself when the block became fatal, and sat in the middle of multiple jury evictions without being the immediate target until final four.
placements.demise: Misha ended Tobias’s game after winning the final-four veto. Joel’s nominations put Misha and Jules up, but Misha’s veto forced Tobias into the only available chair, and she chose to evict him over Jules because Tobias had too many jury relationships and too much endgame credibility.
placements.optimalLine: Once Misha won veto, Tobias needed to make the decision about Jules beating Misha, not Tobias beating Misha. He tried versions of that, but his own jury relationships were too obvious by then.

placements.name: Jane
placements.notes: Jane re-entered through the battle back, rebuilt impressively, but never fully escaped being the expendable returning player.
placements.story: Jane’s game is strange because she effectively starts late, leaves, returns, and still becomes one of the most relevant late-jury players. After entering separately from the twin twist, she built real relationships quickly, especially with Natasha, Gyselle, Joel, Tobias and Felipe. Her record is better than a simple fifth-place boot: she won an HOH and a veto, returned through the battle back, and was involved in the votes that shaped the late game. The problem was agency visibility. She often knew something was moving, but too many of her decisions became other people’s moves — saving Joel with veto, cutting Felipe, losing Natasha, then being protected or discarded by the same rooms. At final five, Misha nominated Jane beside Tobias, won veto, and left the block intact; Joel and Jules then chose to remove Jane because she had enough connections to be dangerous but not enough votes to make herself indispensable. She was never a goat, but she was frequently the available piece.
keyMoments: Week 4: Entered as a separate houseguest after the twin reveal.
Week 7: Evicted 5-4, then later won the battle back over Nico to re-enter.
Week 10: Sat next to Ireland and survived 7-0 when the house chose the comp threat.
Week 12: Won veto and used it on Joel, creating the Gyselle renom and Felipe boot.
Week 13: Won the live double HOH and nominated Misha and Jules before Misha saved herself.
Week 14: Evicted 2-0 over Tobias after Misha left nominations the same.
placements.resume: Jane could claim a battle-back win, an HOH, a veto, several late-game alliances, and a demonstrated ability to rebuild after being evicted. Her honest case was that she adapted better than most people who were forced to play from behind.
placements.demise: Misha put Jane on the block at final five, and Joel and Jules executed the vote. Jane’s mistake was believing the Tobias/Jane bond and Joel/Jane goodwill were enough when Joel and Jules both saw her as the cleaner boot than Tobias.
placements.optimalLine: Jane needed to use her veto debt with Joel earlier and more explicitly to force a Joel/Jules fracture before final five. Waiting to be reassured after the veto meeting was the mistake she named herself.

placements.name: Aaron
placements.notes: Aaron was a loyal soldier with clutch safety wins, but his narrow relationship base finally left him without votes.
placements.story: Aaron’s game was coherent: choose a few people, stay loyal, win when necessary, and let bigger targets absorb fire. That got him very far. He was nominated seven times in the measured record, often as a target, and saved himself in the arena three times, including critical late Block Buster wins. His 89% voting accuracy shows he was usually aligned with the actual house decision, even when he was not portrayed as a mastermind. The downside is that his game was too relationship-light outside his core. When he needed votes at the double eviction, he had not invested enough in the people holding them, and Tobias ultimately chose Jules over him. Aaron’s end was not a collapse; it was the bill for playing most of the season through a small trusted circle.
keyMoments: Week 5: Won veto while nominated and forced Hasan onto the block.
Week 8: Won Block Buster to survive over Nico.
Week 11: Won Block Buster again, escaping the Natasha/Tobias vote.
Week 12: Won HOH but saw the week end with Felipe leaving, not the clean structure he wanted.
Week 13: Won Block Buster, then was renominated in the live double after Misha used veto.
Week 13 double: Evicted 2-1 when Tobias and Misha kept Jules.
placements.resume: Aaron could argue a strong survival résumé: multiple self-saves, a late HOH, high vote accuracy, and loyalty that made him a reliable number rather than a random floater.
placements.demise: Jane’s double-eviction HOH put Misha and Jules up, Misha won veto, and Aaron became the replacement because his comp record and exposed bonds made him the obvious available threat. Misha and Tobias chose to evict him, leaving Joel as the lone vote to keep Jules.
placements.optimalLine: Aaron needed to widen his jury and vote relationships before the double. By the time he was asking for help, people respected him but did not owe him enough.

placements.name: Gyselle
placements.notes: Gyselle was socially embedded everywhere, but her refusal to own hard decisions made her easy to cut when the vote required a name.
placements.story: Gyselle’s numbers show a player with reach: five groups, eight-person reach, and enough social capital to survive deep despite zero HOH or veto wins. She was often positioned as the crack in alliances, which is not automatically bad — it meant she had options. Her problem was that she rarely turned options into ownership. She survived danger through social cushioning and two arena saves, but she was blindsided three times and voted with the house only 70%, indicating she was often near the room rather than inside it. Her betrayal of Hasan was necessary, but it also confirmed to others that her loyalty could be moved without giving her sole credit for the move. At final seven, she sat next to Jane, did not campaign because she thought the count was set, and got evicted when Tobias, Joel and Aaron landed on her as the bigger threat. She had a path, but she needed to claim decisions sooner.
keyMoments: Week 3: Survived against Amberly after the Power Couple protected her.
Week 6: Voted out Hasan despite their final two, breaking the relationship for position.
Week 8: Won Block Buster to escape the block before Nico left.
Week 12: Won Block Buster over Felipe and Jules, forcing the Felipe boot.
Week 13: Lost the arena, assumed the votes were there, and left 3-1 over Jane.
placements.resume: Gyselle could argue that she maintained bonds across nearly every side, survived multiple target weeks, won two Block Busters, and repeatedly became the vote people had to negotiate with.
placements.demise: Misha’s Week 13 HOH nominated Gyselle with Jane and Joel, Joel’s veto removed himself, Aaron went up, then Aaron won Block Buster. Once it was Jane versus Gyselle, Tobias gathered Joel and Aaron around the argument that Gyselle was the larger endgame threat, and Jules was alone on Jane.
placements.optimalLine: Gyselle needed to campaign after losing Block Buster. Her read that there were three votes against her was correct, but treating that as unchangeable let Tobias lock them without resistance.

placements.name: Felipe
placements.notes: Felipe had excellent positioning for most of the game, but his web of final twos finally made him disposable to every side at once.
placements.story: Felipe is one of the better non-winning strategic games despite having no HOH or veto wins. He was nominated only once, as a pawn, voted with the house 90%, and had six groups with eleven-person reach. That is not passive; that is sustained access. For much of the season, Felipe was the person who could move between Jules, Nico, Joel, Aaron, Jane and the larger blocs without being the immediate target. The issue is that his endgame web became too easy to map. Once Nico was gone and Joel/Felipe became visible, he lost the ability to be everybody’s spare number. At Week 12, Jane’s veto saved Joel, Gyselle won the arena, and the vote reduced to Felipe versus Jules. Gyselle and Misha chose the War Room line, Jane signed on, and Felipe’s lack of comp threat did not save him because his relationships were more dangerous than his résumé.
keyMoments: Week 2: Made the early final two with Nico that shaped his first half.
Week 5: Helped recruit Joel onto the Hasan vote while managing multiple rooms.
Week 8: Cut Nico despite their final two, a necessary but costly betrayal.
Week 11: Voted Natasha out in the tie week, further exposing his flexible loyalties.
Week 12: Lost BB Comics to Jane by 2.25 seconds, leaving veto out of reach.
Week 12: Evicted 3-2 over Jules after Jane flipped away from him.
placements.resume: Felipe could argue that he was almost never on the block, voted correctly at an elite rate, sat in nearly every relevant room, and used relationships rather than competitions to stay central for twelve weeks.
placements.demise: Aaron nominated Felipe as a pawn beside Joel and Jules. Jane won veto and used it on Joel, Gyselle went up, then Gyselle won Block Buster. Against Jules, Felipe needed Jane or Misha; Gyselle recruited Jane, Misha stayed with the War Room, and his own overlapping deals made him easier to cut than save.
placements.optimalLine: Felipe needed to choose a visible side after Nico left instead of continuing to sell incompatible endgames. The flexible middle was valuable until every remaining player could compare notes.

placements.name: Natasha
placements.notes: Natasha was a strong social organizer whose loyalty to visible pairs and groups made her a clean tie-break boot.
placements.story: Natasha’s game had real structure from the beginning. She was central to The Power Couple, then The War Room and The Oath, and she maintained a durable social bond with Gyselle after Zella left. Her 63% voting accuracy and three blindsides show the weakness: she often believed the room was where her relationships were, when the room had already shifted somewhere else. She was rarely a comp force, but her Block Buster win in Week 10 was one of the season’s real clutch survival moments because it prevented Ireland from simply staying as the obvious target next to her. The problem came at Week 11, when she sat next to Tobias after Aaron won the arena. Her social game kept the vote tied, but Joel’s HOH tiebreaker chose to remove her, and that says the house saw her as a more disruptive social piece than Tobias in that exact configuration. She was not dragged; she was targeted for being socially useful to too many people.
keyMoments: Week 1: Formed The Power Couple with Gyselle.
Week 3: Deepened the Zella relationship, creating a visible pair that shaped multiple votes.
Week 10: Won Block Buster to escape the block, leaving Jane and Ireland exposed.
Week 10: Helped consolidate the unanimous Ireland eviction.
Week 11: Sat next to Tobias after Aaron saved himself and forced a 3-3 tie.
Week 11: Evicted by Joel's tiebreaker.
placements.resume: Natasha could argue that her social connections repeatedly set vote direction, that she survived long stretches without power because people needed her, and that she won the arena when her game was genuinely on the line.
placements.demise: Joel ended Natasha’s game. After Aaron won Block Buster, the vote split 3-3 between Natasha and Tobias; Joel, as HOH, broke the tie against Natasha because her connections through Gyselle, Jane and the War Room were less useful to his endgame than Tobias staying as a shield and number.
placements.optimalLine: Natasha needed to break from the visible Gyselle/Jane structure earlier or make Joel believe Tobias was the unbeatable jury threat. She had the votes to tie, but not the HOH relationship to survive the tie.

placements.name: Ireland
placements.notes: Ireland was the season’s early comp monster and power user, but once the house stopped needing her as a weapon, they removed her unanimously.
placements.story: Ireland’s raw competition record is absurd for a tenth-place finish: 3 HOHs, 4 vetoes, 3 Block Busters, and repeated wins under threat. But the record also explains the fall. She was on the block six times, all as the target, voted with the house only 40%, and was blindsided three times in just five votes. That means she was powerful, but rarely structurally safe. Her secret power in Week 2 was excellent short-term play, stealing the HOH and reshaping the week, but it also branded her as the person things ended up with. From there, she had to keep winning because trust never recovered. By Week 10, the entire house agreed that the comp threat had to go; Natasha won the arena, Jane stayed passive, and Ireland had no vote coalition left. Her exit is the classic comp-dependent arc: spectacular survival until one result finally does not land.
keyMoments: Week 2: Used The Interrogation to take Nico's HOH anonymously and nominate Stella, Jules and Joel.
Weeks 3-5: Won three consecutive Block Busters to escape danger repeatedly.
Week 6: Won HOH and veto, nominated Hasan, Tobias and Dylon, and survived the Mystery Veto chaos.
Week 7: Won the prizes/punishments veto and saved herself from Joel's block.
Week 9: Won HOH and veto, nominated Aaron, Tobias and Dylon, and sent Dylon out 8-0.
Week 10: Lost Block Buster to Natasha and was evicted 7-0.
placements.resume: Ireland could argue one of the biggest pre-finale competition résumés in the cast: 10 total safety/power wins, repeated self-saves as the target, and multiple HOH weeks where the house had to respond to her instead of ignore her.
placements.demise: Jules’s Week 10 HOH nominated Ireland beside Jane and Misha. Misha won veto, Natasha went up, and then Natasha won Block Buster, leaving Ireland against Jane. Every voting bloc independently landed on Ireland because her comp record was too large and her social capital too damaged.
placements.optimalLine: Ireland needed to use one of her HOH runs to repair relationships rather than prosecute targets. Once every week became Ireland versus the house, she had no path that did not require winning every safety opportunity.

placements.name: Dylon
placements.notes: Dylon built early power and held a secret veto brilliantly, but his threat level and overexposed deals made him the unanimous mid-jury boot.
placements.story: Dylon’s game was strong until it became too visible. He won 2 HOHs and a veto, carried the Mystery Veto until it mattered, and used it in Week 6 to undo Ireland’s settled block and save himself. That was a great television move and a real game move. His problem was the aftermath: everyone now knew he could win, had powers, and was making deals faster than he could maintain them. His voting accuracy was fine at 75%, but the season turned against visible comp-connected bloc players, and Dylon became the cleanest example. Week 9 sealed it: Ireland nominated Aaron, Tobias and Dylon, Tobias won the arena, and every remaining voter chose Dylon over Aaron. Once even his allies could argue he was the threat in front of them, he had no room left.
keyMoments: Week 1: Won the Mystery Veto instead of the public HOH track.
Week 5: Won HOH and nominated Ireland, Aaron and Zella, then watched the week flip onto Zella.
Week 6: Used the Mystery Veto to save himself after Ireland left nominations intact.
Week 8: Won HOH and targeted Ireland, but she vetoed herself and Nico left instead.
Week 9: Sat next to Aaron after Tobias won Block Buster and was evicted unanimously.
placements.resume: Dylon could argue two HOHs, a veto, a successful secret power play, and several weeks where the house had to plan around his ability to win and redirect the block.
placements.demise: Ireland nominated Dylon with Aaron and Tobias in Week 9. Tobias won Block Buster, and the vote became Dylon versus Aaron. Tobias, Gyselle, Natasha, Joel, Jules, Misha, Jane and Felipe all converged on Dylon because he was the more active, more proven threat.
placements.optimalLine: After using the Mystery Veto, Dylon needed to disappear behind someone else’s target. Instead he kept building and advertising structures, which made the unanimous vote too easy.

placements.name: Nico
placements.notes: Nico was stable and trusted until the end of the pre-jury phase, but he waited too long to launch the move he needed.
placements.story: Nico had a real social game, especially through Felipe, but his measured record shows passivity at the wrong times. He had one HOH that was stolen by Ireland’s secret power, one Block Buster save, and only one official nomination before the week he left. That is a decent defensive game. The issue is that his strongest relationship became a liability once Felipe needed to prove independence, and Nico had no secondary bloc willing to risk itself for him. When Dylon’s Week 8 target on Ireland failed because Ireland won veto, Nico became the replacement as a comp/resume name the room could justify. He did not campaign because he believed the number was set; it was set, just not for him. Felipe voting him out turned a good social bond into the season’s cleanest betrayal.
keyMoments: Week 2: Won the public HOH before Ireland secretly took it from him.
Week 6: Won Block Buster after Dylon's Mystery Veto renommed him, escaping the vote.
Week 8: Renominated after Ireland saved herself with veto.
Week 8: Did not campaign, trusting the count against Aaron.
Week 8: Evicted 6-2 after Felipe cut their Week 1 final two.
placements.resume: Nico could argue loyalty, low threat level, a Block Buster self-save, and enough social trust that his eviction required close allies to betray him.
placements.demise: Dylon nominated Gyselle, Aaron and Ireland; Ireland won veto, so Dylon renamed Nico. Gyselle won Block Buster, leaving Aaron and Nico, and Tobias/Jules/Misha/Ireland/Felipe/Natasha moved onto Nico while he stayed too calm to disrupt the count.
placements.optimalLine: Nico needed to campaign aggressively the moment he became the replacement nominee. His read that calmness protected him was exactly what let people vote him out without fearing blowback.

placements.name: Hasan
placements.notes: Hasan understood vote structure early, but his HOH created enemies he could not out-organize once he lost power.
placements.story: Hasan’s early game had promise. He won the Week 3 HOH, used it to target Amberly and expose parts of The Power Couple, and was involved in multiple core structures. His problem was that his relationships did not survive pressure: Gyselle, his final two, eventually voted him out, and the people he thought were numbers became people comparing his stories. He was nominated twice, once as target and once as renom, and survived one vote before the house had enough. By Week 6, after Dylon’s Mystery Veto forced Nico up and Nico saved himself, Hasan was left sitting next to Tobias. The house chose to keep Tobias as the more useful connected piece and remove Hasan 9-1. He did not lose because he was useless; he lost because his power week made him legible before his social bonds were strong enough.
keyMoments: Week 3: Won HOH and nominated Amberly, Gyselle and Ireland.
Week 3: Put Gyselle up as a pawn, damaging the relationship that was supposed to protect him.
Week 5: Renominated after Aaron used veto, then survived when Zella left 6-5.
Week 6: Sat on Ireland's block, survived Dylon's Mystery Veto chaos, but lost against Tobias 9-1.
placements.resume: Hasan could argue that he won power early, identified real blocs before others acted on them, and survived a close Week 5 vote despite being a replacement nominee.
placements.demise: Ireland nominated Hasan, Tobias and Dylon in Week 6. Dylon’s Mystery Veto removed Dylon and forced Nico up, then Nico won Block Buster. Against Tobias, Hasan lost because Dylon’s Dock Pact/Assembly structure, plus outsiders like Natasha, Joel, Jules and Jane, all agreed Hasan was less useful and more damaged.
placements.optimalLine: Hasan needed to repair Gyselle immediately after using her as a pawn and stop pushing Ireland stories that other people could fact-check. His correct path was humility after HOH, not more control.

placements.name: Zella
placements.notes: Zella played visibly and loyally, but her showmance and blunt style gave the house an easy mid-prejury cut.
placements.story: Zella’s game was never subtle, and that was both the appeal and the flaw. She won a Block Buster, survived early danger, and was central to the Natasha relationship that shaped the first half of the house. But by Week 5, the house could see that keeping Zella meant keeping a visible pair and a loud strategic presence. She was nominated twice, both as the target, and had no ability to soften the target once the vote became Hasan versus Zella. The 6-5 vote shows she had a path — this was not a hopeless position — but she did not campaign enough because she believed the count was locked. Misha’s vote and Gyselle/Jane’s positioning ended her. Her exit accusation against Misha was right, but it came when she no longer had a vote.
keyMoments: Week 2: Renominated by Ireland, then won Block Buster to escape the vote.
Week 3: Made the Natasha final two/showmance structure visible enough for the house to clock it.
Week 5: Sat against Hasan after Ireland won Block Buster.
Week 5: Did not campaign hard, believing the numbers were there.
Week 5: Evicted 6-5 and correctly named Misha on the way out.
placements.resume: Zella could argue loyalty, a self-save under pressure, and influence through The Power Couple and Natasha, but her résumé was more about visibility than executed control.
placements.demise: After Dylon nominated Ireland, Aaron and Zella, Aaron vetoed himself and Hasan went up. Ireland won Block Buster, leaving Hasan and Zella. Misha, Gyselle, Jane, Tobias, Joel and Jules formed the decisive six to evict Zella while she thought Hasan was leaving.
placements.optimalLine: Zella needed to treat the Hasan vote as live until the last ballot, not as settled. Her best move was exposing Misha before eviction night rather than at the door.

placements.name: Harriett
placements.notes: Harriett’s twin twist gave her a second vote in the game, but her own deal-making became too contradictory to survive scrutiny.
placements.story: Harriett’s game had an unusual opening because the twin twist delayed Jane’s full entry while making every Harriett conversation unstable in retrospect. Strategically, though, Harriett did not convert the twist into durable power. She had one group, won no standard comps, and left before jury after being exposed as telling too many people too many different versions of the plan. The Week 4 Mystery Competitor power bought a veto draw body, not safety, and Scott losing meant the power produced attention without protection. Once Jules held HOH and the house compared Harriett’s stories, the vote became unanimous. She was not an early nobody; she was an early overplayer. The house removed her because her information game had become visible and unreliable.
keyMoments: Week 1: Entered as the public half of the twin twist while Jane stayed hidden.
Week 2: Formed The Pipeline with Stella, then voted against the alliance direction.
Week 4: The twin reveal brought Jane into the house and reset how everyone viewed Harriett's conversations.
Week 4: Used Mystery Competitor to bring Scott into the veto draw, but got no safety.
Week 4: Exposed by multiple houseguests comparing contradictory stories and evicted 12-0.
placements.resume: Harriett could argue that she survived the twin twist long enough to bring Jane into the game and made early deals across the house, but she had no meaningful eviction-control case.
placements.demise: Jules nominated Harriett, Natasha and Ireland. Ireland won Block Buster, leaving Harriett against Natasha. By then Dylon, Felipe, Ireland, Jules and Misha had all compared Harriett’s conflicting stories, and every bloc preferred removing the exposed liar over the visible Natasha/Zella pair.
placements.optimalLine: Harriett needed to simplify after the twin reveal. Instead of continuing to sell different stories, she should have picked one defensible alliance and made the twist itself the shield.

placements.name: Amberly
placements.notes: Amberly had real social instincts but mistook personal warmth for votes that would risk themselves for her.
placements.story: Amberly was socially active from the start and had enough presence that her eviction mattered. She was not dragged out because she was irrelevant; she was removed because people could see she might become a problem. Her mistake was believing that being liked and being protected were the same thing. Hasan’s HOH put her on the block beside Gyselle and Ireland, and once Ireland won Block Buster, Amberly was left against a better-insulated alliance member. The vote was 10-2 because The Power Couple and its attached numbers had more structure than Amberly’s looser personal ties. Her door warning about Gyselle, Natasha, Zella, Felipe, Hasan and Misha was accurate, which is the tragedy: she saw the house, but too late to make the house act.
keyMoments: Week 1: Built broad early personal relationships but was left out of actual plans.
Week 2: Benefited from Ireland's secret HOH safety deal but remained outside the core.
Week 3: Nominated by Hasan as a target.
Week 3: Campaigned against The Power Couple structure but could not crack it.
Week 3: Evicted 10-2 and accurately exposed the majority on the way out.
placements.resume: Amberly could argue she identified the main power structure before most people were willing to say it aloud and had enough social pull to force others to account for her, but she had no comp wins or vote-control résumé.
placements.demise: Hasan nominated Amberly with Gyselle and Ireland. Dylon left the veto unused, Ireland won Block Buster, and the Power Couple plus attached voters protected Gyselle. Amberly’s looser social ties could not beat an organized group vote.
placements.optimalLine: Amberly needed to name the power structure before she was on the block, not at the door. Once nominated beside Gyselle, she had to make keeping her the anti-majority vote immediately.

placements.name: Stella
placements.notes: Stella’s loyal early bonds were not enough once the house decided she was the clean first eviction.
placements.story: Stella went out before the season’s real structures hardened, so there is a limit to the game case. She built a meaningful bond with Harriett and had enough trust with Tobias that his vote against her counted as a broken promise. But she did not have a backup plan when Ireland’s secret HOH put her on the block with Jules and Joel. Joel won veto, Zella went up, Zella won Block Buster, and Stella was left against Jules, who had more active campaign routes and more people willing to keep him as a game piece. The 10-3 vote shows Stella did not just narrowly miss; she badly misread how many votes had already moved. Her game was loyalty-forward, but loyalty in Week 2 needed a vote count attached.
keyMoments: Week 1: Built The Pipeline bond with Harriett.
Week 2: Nominated by Ireland's secret HOH alongside Jules and Joel.
Week 2: Did not campaign enough after Zella won Block Buster.
Week 2: Evicted 10-3 after believing the vote was closer.
Week 8: Lost the first battle-back round to Amberly.
placements.resume: Stella had no real finale case. Her honest argument would be that she built genuine loyalty quickly, but she left before she could turn it into power.
placements.demise: Ireland’s Week 2 secret HOH nominated Stella, Jules and Joel. Joel won veto, Zella became the renom, Zella saved herself in Block Buster, and the house chose to keep Jules as the more useful player while Tobias and others abandoned Stella.
placements.optimalLine: Stella needed to campaign after the Block Buster instead of trusting the relationships she already had. Her best available pitch was that Jules was the more dangerous long-term social player.

twists.name: No Eviction
twists.desc: No nomination ceremony, no veto and no vote: the house is the same size on Thursday as it was on Sunday. The Head of Household competition still runs and still crowns somebody, which leaves one houseguest holding the most powerful seat in the game with absolutely nothing to spend it on — and everybody else with a week to work in and no ceremony to be judged by. Pairs with anything hiding inside the competition, because a week that cannot evict anybody is a week whose only outcome is who walked away holding something.

twists.name: Secret Power Competition
twists.desc: Three powers are hidden inside this week's Head of Household competition, and before a single houseguest plays they decide in private what they are actually competing for: the crown, or one of the three. Not both. The outgoing Head of Household cannot win the crown back and so plays only for a power, which is the one week their exclusion is worth something. Somebody out there is about to post the best score of the afternoon and not be Head of Household, because that was never what they were running for — and the house will spend weeks not understanding why. Winners are told alone and nothing is announced. Every power won here dies the moment the jury opens, which is why they are allowed to be this strong.

twists.name: Have-Nots
twists.desc: The new Head of Household puts part of the house on slop, cold showers and the have-not room for the week. Have-nots compete at a real disadvantage in the veto, and nobody forgets who chose them.

twists.name: The Twin Twist
twists.desc: One houseguest was secretly two people swapping places every week. Harriett and Jane played as one, and lasted long enough to both enter the game as individuals in week 4.

twists.name: Prizes and Punishments
twists.desc: The veto competition stops awarding the veto and starts deciding who picks first. Everybody then chooses a wrapped box: the Power of Veto is in one of them, and the rest hold cash, a holiday, a call home, a bag of confetti, or a punishment nobody wants. Finish last in the competition and you pick first, blind; win it and you pick last, with every opened box on the table and stealable. Anything stolen once is frozen and can never be taken again, so the veto changes hands in public until somebody makes it stop — and every season this format runs, somebody on the block chooses the money.

twists.name: Something In This House
twists.desc: A real power is hidden somewhere in the house — behind the cereal, under a have-not bed, in the HOH cistern — and the house is told only that it exists. No clue, no competition, no map. The only way to hold it is to go and look, and looking is not a private act: a houseguest seen rummaging is a houseguest who visibly believes there is something to find, which costs them and makes everybody else start looking too. Whoever finds it is told nothing publicly. If nobody finds it in four evictions it is taken away and the house never learns it was there.

twists.name: Battle Back
twists.desc: The evicted houseguests are not gone. After this week's eviction they compete for the right to walk back in — as a gauntlet, where the first evictee must beat every person who followed them out, or as a Showdown, where the survivor still has to get past a champion the house elects to hold the door shut. The winner re-enters with no immunity and a complete memory of who voted them out.

twists.name: Double Eviction
twists.desc: Two evictions in one night. The week plays normally, and the moment the first houseguest walks out the house runs a second, compressed cycle live: new Head of Household, nominations, veto and vote with no time to campaign properly. Two people leave.

seasonNarrative: Season 1 was not a clean steamroll; the plan held only 5 times and broke 10. The defining strategic pattern was that every alliance became public before it became safe. The Power Couple, Dock Pact, Assembly, War Room, Oath, Drama Club and Double Edge all had moments of influence, but none survived comparison of notes for long. Competition wins mattered, especially for Ireland, Joel, Misha and Dylon, yet the season was ultimately decided by who could survive after power expired. Ireland and Dylon show the danger of being a visible comp engine without enough social trust; Felipe and Jane show the danger of having too many deals with no final ownership; Tobias shows the strength and ceiling of being a hub everyone likes but everyone can identify. The final vote distilled the whole season: Jules represented trust, relationship and social repair; Misha represented adaptive survival, clutch safety and the willingness to make the last hard cut. The jury split almost perfectly along that line, and Misha won because one more juror respected the game that kept reassembling itself around her.

bestStrategic.name: Misha
bestStrategic.description: Misha gets the strategic award because her game kept surviving contact with exposure. She was implicated in major votes, targeted multiple times, and still reached the end with enough jury respect to beat a beloved finalist.

bestSocial.name: Jules
bestSocial.description: Jules’s social game was the cleanest pure relationship engine of the season. Four target nominations and four vote survivals is the evidence: people kept choosing him when they had the chance not to.

bestPhysical.name: Ireland
bestPhysical.description: Ireland was the season’s most overwhelming physical/endurance-adjacent presence when counting HOH, veto and Block Buster output, even if the same résumé made her impossible to keep.

mostClutch.name: Misha
mostClutch.description: Misha’s late-game veto and final HOH wins came with her actual life in the game on the line. The final-four veto and finale tiebreaker are the definition of clutch.

mostLoyal.name: Aaron
mostLoyal.description: Aaron’s loyalty was not always optimal, but it was consistent. He kept choosing his people even when broader social investment would have helped him more.

bestUnderdog.name: Jane
bestUnderdog.description: Jane entered late, got evicted, battled back, and still reached fifth with real relationships and a veto win. That is the season’s best underdog arc.

biggestVillain.name: Misha
biggestVillain.description: Misha was not cartoonishly villainous, but the winner’s path ran through betrayals jurors felt personally. Owning the screens at the reunion sealed the role.

mostChaotic.name: Ireland
mostChaotic.description: Ireland’s game was constant motion: stolen HOH, repeated self-saves, blown-up promises, public confrontations, and a comp résumé that made every week about her.

quietestThreat.name: Felipe
quietestThreat.description: Felipe was almost never in danger and was in almost every room. The threat was quiet because it looked like listening until the final twos started colliding.

seasonMVP.name: Misha
seasonMVP.description: Misha wins MVP because she combined the winning vote, the most important late competitions, and the decisive final cut. The season’s endgame runs through her.

mostTragic.name: Joel
mostTragic.description: Joel was one final jury-quiz tiebreaker from choosing his opponent and possibly winning. Instead, the person he needed to beat cut him one chair short.

mostUnlucky.name: Felipe
mostUnlucky.description: Felipe losing BB Comics to Jane by 2.25 seconds directly set up the veto chain that ended his game. A tiny margin became a jury seat.

ironPerson.name: Misha
ironPerson.description: Misha lasted the full season, survived repeated danger, won multiple high-pressure comps, and still had enough stamina to take Part 1 and Part 3 of the final HOH.

biggestMeltdown.name: Ireland
biggestMeltdown.description: Ireland’s late HOH overplay and public certainty around Dylon turned the house’s fear of her into a unanimous eviction plan the very next week.

gold.name: Misha
gold.description: Winner, six HOH/veto wins, final HOH, final cut, and the jury respect to beat Jules 5-4.

silver.name: Jules
silver.description: The strongest social game of the season and one vote away from winning, with repeated survival as the target.

gold.name: Tobias
gold.description: America’s Favorite and the houseguest most often treated with affection even by people plotting against him.

silver.name: Jules
silver.description: Jules’s care work, cooking, and loyalty-based social game made him the emotional center for much of the cast.

gold.name: Misha
gold.description: The winner owned multiple hidden votes and betrayals at the reunion and still won, making her the season’s most effective villain.

silver.name: Ireland
silver.description: Ireland’s power-heavy, confrontational style made her the house’s favorite target and antagonist through the middle game.

gold.name: Ireland
gold.description: Three HOHs, four vetoes and three Block Busters made Ireland the season’s biggest total comp presence.

silver.name: Joel
silver.description: Three HOHs and three vetoes, with key endgame wins that forced everyone to plan around him.

gold.name: Jules
gold.description: Jules repeatedly survived target nominations because enough people still wanted him in the house.

silver.name: Felipe
silver.description: Felipe’s low nomination count and huge alliance reach made him the best quiet social connector.

gold.name: Misha
gold.description: Misha’s strategic strength was timing: she rarely had total control, but she knew when to attach, when to cut, and when to win.

silver.name: Tobias
silver.description: Tobias stood in the middle of several jury evictions and kept rebuilding his structure after each betrayal.

gold.name: Joel
gold.description: Joel lost the final HOH tiebreaker, got cut by Misha, and became the last juror after being one decision from the final two.

silver.name: Nico
silver.description: Nico was blindsided 6-2, then lost the battle back to Jane immediately after becoming the first juror.

gold.name: Ireland
gold.description: Ireland’s Interrogation power stole an HOH and set the tone for the season’s secret-power paranoia.

silver.name: Dylon
silver.description: Dylon’s Mystery Veto was held until it mattered and blew up a settled Week 6 block.

gold.name: Joel
gold.description: Joel was not twist-robbed, but he was game-robbed in the purest sense: one question from control, then cut because he could win.

gold.name: Jules
gold.description: Jules answered the jury better on several relationship questions and converted a bitter Joel into a vote, but it was not quite enough.

gold.name: Jules
gold.description: Jules lost 5-4 despite a finalist case many jurors openly admired. One vote flips and the season reads as a social-masterclass win.

messiestFeud.description: Misha and Jane’s feud kept regenerating from overheard plans, food, beds, vote suspicion and mutual distrust, long after the original causes stopped mattering.

biggestBetrayal.description: Misha cutting Joel at final three was the season’s decisive betrayal: personal, strategic, and directly responsible for her win.

secondBiggestBetrayal.description: Felipe voting out Nico broke the Week 1 final two and proved that even the season’s most sincere early bond had an expiration date.

legacyMoment.name: Misha cuts Joel
legacyMoment.description: Misha winning the final HOH and choosing Jules over Joel is the moment that decided the season and reframed her entire game as intentional rather than merely survivable.

fanFavorite.name: Tobias
fanFavorite.description: Tobias was voted the house's favourite by the audience.

villainBoard.read: Misha did the most to other people this season, and Ireland was not far behind.
